transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-10-29 14:30 UTC
Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Anika (Redwood Sec), Priya (Cedar Head Sec), Liam (Cedar Cloud), Sara (Cedar Compliance), Jon (Cedar Infra)
Links shared: https://redwood.example.com/security/cedar-network-design-v1.pdf, https://redwood.example.com/poC/egress-runbook.xlsx

Summary:
Quick kickoff to align on geo-fencing/data residency and perimeter controls for a private deploy (VPC + optional on-prem package). Goal: agree on PoC scope (egress gateway performance, KMS integration, RBAC/SAML SSO, audit log shipping), identify blockers for SOC2/ISO evidence, and gather network diagrams.

Topics:
- Data residency: region scoping and legal constraints
- Network isolation: ingress/egress models, NAT, private endpoints
- Firewalling and segmentation: microsegmentation expectations
- KMS/encryption: bring-your-own-key, rotation, HSM support
- RBAC/SSO and audit logs: SAML, SCIM, log retention and SIEM integrations
- PoC plan: benchmark and runbook

Action items (captured above)

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Okay hi everyone, thanks for joining. This is Maya from Redwood — we, um, wanted to run through the geo-fencing and perimeter security piece for the private deployment. Diego and Anika are with me, Diego will cover the egress/gateway perf, and Anika will do the SSO/KMS stuff.
[00:18] Priya: Great, thanks. We're most concerned about two things: one is data residency for PHI-ish analytics buckets, and two is making sure audit logs and SSO meet our SOC2 evidence. We're trying not to re-invent the network model.
[00:32] Diego: Quick note — we call the private product 'Redwood Private' but sometimes the docs use Redboard or Redwoode in older exports, ignore that. The architecture we propose supports either a VPC-hosted private control plane or a fully customer-hosted control plane if you need air-gapped.
[00:48] Liam: For Cedar, we need region locking: EU only for EU customers, and US-only for persons in US datasets. We also have a handful of customers in APAC, but those are lower priority. We need to confirm the egress points won't accidentally route EU traffic through US-based analytics.
[01:05] Anika: For region locking we have two options: 1) policy-based routing where requests get pinned by tenant to specific routing table and egress gateway, or 2) physically separate clusters per region. Each has tradeoffs on cost and complexity.
[01:22] Jon: Physically separate clusters sounds safest but will cost more and complicate model version sync. Are there ways to ensure logical separation and still get auditability?
[01:35] Diego: Yes, you can do logical tenancy with strict tagging and enforced egress via a customer-owned egress NAT with strict route table rules. That way logs show customer-owned egress IPs. We can also set up prefix lists so only approved destinations are allowed.
[01:52] Priya: About logs — we need immutable audit logs shipped to our SIEM, retention 7 years for some regs. Can Redwood stream logs to an S3 bucket in our account or push to our SIEM via syslog/Kafka?
[02:08] Anika: We support pushing audit logs to a customer-managed S3 bucket (server-side encrypted with your KMS), plus direct forwarders to syslog or Kafka. There are slight timing/perf differences — we can show throughput numbers in the PoC.
[02:25] Sara: And what about evidence for SOC2: do you provide an inventory of controls, and is your control mapping to CC2/CC6 available?
[02:34] Maya: Yes, we'll share the SOC2 control mapping doc and the ISO-27001 summary. We'll also include the audit log retention and encryption sections. I'll send the questionnaire after the call.
[02:45] Liam: Can we talk about ingress? We run private endpoints and want to avoid public internet exposure. What's the recommended model?
[02:55] Diego: Two recommended models: Private load balancer with VPC endpoints (no public LB), or a bastion/jumpbox into a private management network. For model runtime, we typically use private endpoints with mTLS between customer infra and model nodes, and customers can terminate TLS at their perimeter if they prefer.
[03:12] Jon: mTLS between our internal LB and your runtime — do you support client certs from our PKI, or do you require Redwood-managed certs?
[03:21] Anika: We support customer-provided certs, and can integrate with your internal PKI — for the on-prem package we can accept mutual TLS certs signed by your CA. For cloud VPC we can also integrate via ACM or your KMS-wrapped certs.
[03:36] Priya: KMS detail — we need BYOK (bring your own key), HSM-backed rotation, and key export restrictions. Is rotation automatic or does it require service restart?
[03:48] Diego: Rotation is seamless for most keys; we do envelope encryption — data keys are rewrapped by the new key, and the runtime can handle KV cache migration without full restarts in most cases. For HSM-backed KMS, we support AWS CloudHSM + KMS, GCP CMEK, and customer on-prem HSM via KMIP in the on-prem package.
[04:08] Priya: Any caveats on latency when using remote HSMs?
[04:12] Diego: Slight overhead — typically single-digit milliseconds for KMS calls. For high throughput token generation you can cache data keys in a local secure enclave; we recommend running a short-lived cache to balance perf and key rotation policies. We'll include recommended TTLs in the PoC doc.
[04:32] Liam: Firewall rules — we need explicit egress deny-by-default and allow lists for model download, telemetry endpoints, and package repositories. Can Redwood work with strict deny-all and only open specific prefixes?
[04:46] Maya: Yes, Redwood supports deny-by-default. For model downloads we can host model artifacts in customer-owned staging S3 or pre-seed model files in your network to avoid external pulls. For telemetry/heartbeat, we can provide a small list of endpoints and IP ranges to allow.
[05:04] Jon: What about OS-level patching and image provenance for the on-prem nodes? We need SBOM and signed images.
[05:12] Anika: We provide SBOMs for all runtime images and sign them. For on-prem, we provide image manifest and attestations you can verify during deployment. We can also support a supply-chain attestation via Sigstore if you require.
[05:28] Priya: On RBAC and SSO: we use SAML2 for SSO and SCIM for user provisioning. We also need role separation so that platform operators cannot read raw log bodies for PII. How do you handle RBAC scoping?
[05:44] Anika: We integrate with SAML for auth and SCIM for provisioning. RBAC rules are hierarchical and you can scope to token-level or route-level. For very sensitive data we recommend token scoping + KMS policies that prevent decryption unless the call is from an approved tenant. Also, audit logs can redact PII before shipping if you enable log scrubbing rules.
[06:03] Sara: Log scrubbing — is that configurable by regex? We need to ensure PHI fields are masked before logs leave our environment.
[06:12] Diego: Yes, we have configurable log transforms; you can run scrubbing at your side before shipping or within the runtime. The recommended approach for PHI is to scrub at the source and ship only meta-events to Redwood's control plane.
[06:28] Priya: About evidence for auditors — will you provide a runbook showing how RBAC changes are audited, and can we pull a changelog for user role changes over the last 12 months?
[06:40] Maya: We can surface role change events in the audit log with user, timestamp, and diff payload. We'll include an example export in the SOC2 pack.
[06:50] Liam: Performance for egress gateway — Diego, can you summarize the expected throughput and latencies if we use a customer-managed egress gateway in us-east and eu-west?
[06:58] Diego: Sure — for a standard N4-ish instance we see median added latency of 8–15ms per request for TLS termination and routing. Throughput depends on instance sizing; in the PoC we'll run concurrent token-generation workloads to show tokens/sec and 95th pct latency. If you need <20ms p95 we recommend colocating egress points with model runtime and using optimized TLS stacks.
[07:20] Jon: For the PoC we want to run 2 scenarios: one with satellite logical tenancy (shared cluster, tagged routing) and one with a physically separated cluster in eu-west. We will measure latency, cost delta, and failover behavior.
[07:33] Maya: That sounds good. We'll prepare a runbook and test harness. Diego will own the egress perf runs, Anika will own RBAC/SAML and KMS rotation tests.
[07:44] Priya: Any blockers on our side? We'll need to provide keys and a sandbox account in the EU region. Also legal needs the data flow diagram for sign-off.
[07:54] Maya: We'll add the network diagram to the materials (see link earlier). If you can share your current firewall rules and subnet ranges, Jon, we will map the required exceptions.
[08:03] Jon: I'll export the firewall policy and send it to Maya. Expect it by Monday.
[08:09] Sara: One more question on SIEM — do you do guaranteed delivery to our Kafka cluster? We don't want log loss during pipeline failures.
[08:18] Anika: We support at-least-once delivery with retry buffers; for Kafka we can configure partitions and consumer groups to achieve durable delivery. We also provide a dead-letter queue pattern if your SIEM is temporarily unavailable.
[08:32] Priya: Good. Last thing — can you outline how access is revoked when an employee leaves? We need SCIM deprovisioning plus immediate token revocation.
[08:41] Maya: Yes, SCIM deprovisioning plus immediate token revocation is supported. We can demonstrate token invalidation in the RBAC test during PoC.
[08:50] Liam: Ok thanks. I think we have enough to scope the PoC.
[08:55] Maya: Recap quick: Redwood to send SOC2/ISO docs and runbook; customer to send network diagrams and dataset matrix; schedule PoC for week of 11/9. We'll follow up with calendar invites and a detailed test plan.
[09:08] Priya: Thanks everyone, appreciate it.
[09:11] Diego: Thanks, bye.

Notes on transcription: some vendor/product names mis-typed by ASR (Redwood Private sometimes appears as Redboard Private). There was a short network dropout at ~00:50 causing a 3s gap.
